rv.q: The conversation that comes out when these guys sit down and try to figure it all out is an art in itself.
Mr. Hall's play is a touching and thoughtful examination of the intersection of art and class, bringing dignity and complexity to characters who might easily have been patronized or sentimentalized.
Her fluidly staged treatment is both a saucy riff on and an endearing homage to Noel Coward's tale.

In fact, there's only one significant difference between them: "The Pitmen Painters" is good. Not great, you understand, so don't be fooled by the near-hysterical quotes from London's critical corps that have been trotted out as sucker bait for Manhattan theatergoers.
The art in 'The Pitmen Painters' remains, like the play, illustrative, informative and confined to its frame.
Here, the art in question is painting, and the play's initial brushstrokes are light and funny before it grows darker and more political in the second half.
It’s uncynical and forthright, like its subjects, and when Hall finally gets into the sticky question of exploitation—are the pitmen truly artists?

All of the men (and the two women) in this well-acted British production, imported to Broadway by the Manhattan Theater Club with its original director (Max Roberts) and cast, have surface traits and quirks to call their own.
Unfortunately, despite fine performances, "Pitmen Painters" is mild-mannered, talky and scattershot.
Playwright Lee Hall's brilliant script captures truly authentic voices in all their prickly, naive glory.
The Pitmen Painters, for the most part, a feel-good charmer that realistically celebrates unexpected human creativity.
That buildup is so satisfying that the last-minute careening off the road matters surprisingly little.

Lee Hall's 'The Pitmen Painters' is a bit like the art made by its characters: Whatever it lacks in technique it more than makes up for in expression. If the characters are sometimes too predictable and the sentiment a bit thick, that doesn't prevent the two-and-a-half-hour play from being thoroughly entertaining.
Despite the glibly drawn characters, the all-English ensemble, under Max Roberts's crisp direction, performs with stirring conviction
Generally, though, Pitmen Painters' imitation of life is something less than art.
The language can suddenly switch from country bumpkin to a level of sophistication well beyond the credible
We get to see their paintings in this inventive production by director Max Robert that audiences will savor.
It is truly our good fortune that the entire original English cast has traveled with the Max Roberts' detailed production to Broadway.

Fairly absorbing in content, Hall's patchy drama about plain blokes transformed by art is somewhat by-the-numbers in its episodic construction, complete with a comedy scene involving a nude model (Lisa McGrillis).
Such poetic license in telling a story that spans some 14 years is expected.

cn.t: Lee Hall's fact-based play about working-class miners discovering art earns warm if measured praise for its heartfelt performances and thoughtful class themes, though critics note predictable plotting and uneven pacing.
